# Getting started
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/docs/getting-started/

Documentation

Getting started

This guide takes you from nothing to a running Fendlemark console connected to at least one of your existing ML platform tools. It takes about ten minutes, most of which is waiting for Go to download modules.

## Requirements

 - Go 1.23 or later to install the CLI. Prebuilt binaries are distributed to Keepers and Stewards following each Silence Period; see release governance.

 - Network access from the machine running Fendlemark to at least one of: an MLflow tracking server, a Metaflow metadata service, an Argo Server, or a Kubeflow Pipelines API endpoint.

 - Node.js 20 or later, only if you intend to develop the console itself. The released binary embeds a built console.

 - A webcam, if you enable Respiratory Identity. Local development runs with authentication disabled by default.

## 1. Install the CLI

```
$ go install fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark/cmd/fendlemark@latest
$ fendlemark version
fendlemark 0.9.4 (go1.23.2, linux/amd64)
console: embedded, built 2026-09-30
```

The module path fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark is a vanity import path served by this site. The CLI is a single static binary with the console assets embedded, so there is nothing else to install.

## 2. Scaffold a project

```
$ fendlemark init my-platform
$ cd my-platform
$ ls
fendlemark.yaml README.md
```

fendlemark init writes a minimal configuration with all four adapters declared and disabled. You enable the ones you have. The generated file is deliberately short; every option has a sensible default, and the configuration reference documents all of them.

## 3. Connect your tools

Open fendlemark.yaml and enable the adapters for the systems you run. A typical first configuration points at an MLflow tracking server and an Argo Workflows namespace:

```
server:
 listen: "127.0.0.1:7411"

adapters:
 mlflow:
 enabled: true
 tracking_uri: "http://mlflow.internal:5000"
 argo:
 enabled: true
 server: "https://argo.internal:2746"
 namespaces: ["ml-training", "ml-batch"]
 metaflow:
 enabled: false
 kubeflow:
 enabled: false
```

Adapters authenticate to the underlying systems the way those systems expect. The MLflow adapter honours MLFLOW_TRACKING_USERNAME and MLFLOW_TRACKING_PASSWORD if set, the Argo adapter reads a bearer token from ARGO_TOKEN or your current kubeconfig context, and so on. Each adapter's page in the adapters reference lists exactly what it reads.

## 4. Check connectivity

```
$ fendlemark adapters check
ADAPTER STATUS LATENCY DETAIL
mlflow healthy 41ms 12 experiments, 1,406 runs visible
argo healthy 88ms 2 namespaces, 37 workflows (4 running)
metaflow disabled
kubeflow disabled
```

If an adapter reports degraded or unreachable, fendlemark doctor will tell you why in more words than you want.

## 5. Start the console

```
$ fendlemark serve
2026-10-24T09:12:03Z INF fendlemark 0.9.4 starting
2026-10-24T09:12:03Z INF adapter mlflow connected tracking_uri=http://mlflow.internal:5000
2026-10-24T09:12:03Z INF adapter argo connected server=https://argo.internal:2746 namespaces=2
2026-10-24T09:12:04Z INF lattice initial reconciliation complete entities=1443 correlations=312 took=612ms
2026-10-24T09:12:04Z INF console listening on http://localhost:7411
```

Open http://localhost:7411. You will see the Overview view: every run, workflow, and model from every enabled adapter, already correlated. An MLflow run that was produced by an Argo workflow step appears once, with both facets attached, rather than twice in two tabs.

 ●

 
 What just happened

 Fendlemark asked each adapter for its facets, then ran the lattice reconciler, which matches entities across tools using correlation keys (an Argo workflow name recorded as an MLflow tag, a Metaflow run id in a Kubeflow pipeline parameter, and so on). The console renders the lattice, not the tools.

 

## Next steps

 

### Architecture
The control plane, adapters, the lattice, and the console, and how a request moves between them.

 

### Configuration
Every key in fendlemark.yaml, including the ones you should not touch.

 

### Adapters
What each built-in adapter reads, what it surfaces, and what it deliberately leaves alone.

 

### Authentication
Respiratory Identity: how the console recognises you, and why it is off by default.

---

# Migrating from 0.8 to 0.9
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/docs/migration/

Documentation

Migrating from 0.8 to 0.9

Fendlemark 0.9.0 renamed one configuration key. This guide exists because the Keepers hold that every breaking change, however small, deserves a document proportionate to the trust it asks of you.

## Summary of changes

0.8 | 0.9 | Type | 

adapters.mlflow.trackingUri | adapters.mlflow.tracking_uri | Renamed | 

That is the complete list. The old spelling is accepted with a deprecation warning (DOC-104) through the 0.9 series and will be removed in 0.10.

## Why

Every other key in fendlemark.yaml is snake_case. trackingUri was camelCase because the first Keeper wrote it at 02:14 on 11 March 2023 while copying the name from MLflow's Python client, and nobody noticed for two and a half years. When it was noticed, it was raised as a Pre-Intent Notice, discussed across three Reflection Periods, and resolved in FDR-041, which also records the Keepers' view that "a single inconsistency in a correct system is not a small thing; it is the only thing".

## Before you begin

 - Confirm you are on 0.8.2 or later. Earlier 0.8 releases should first upgrade to 0.8.2, which changed nothing but was released anyway.

 - Back up fendlemark.yaml. fendlemark doctor --fix does this for you, but the Keepers prefer that you do it yourself, once, deliberately.

 - Read the Philosophy. Not for the migration. For you.

## Migration

### Automatic

```
$ fendlemark doctor --fix
config warn DOC-104 adapters.mlflow.trackingUri is the pre-0.9 spelling; use tracking_uri (fixable)
 fixed renamed adapters.mlflow.trackingUri → adapters.mlflow.tracking_uri
 backup fendlemark.yaml.bak-20261024T091203Z
```

### Manual

```
adapters:
 mlflow:
 enabled: true
- trackingUri: "http://mlflow.internal:5000"
+ tracking_uri: "http://mlflow.internal:5000"
```

### Environment variable form

```
# before
FENDLEMARK_ADAPTERS__MLFLOW__TRACKINGURI=http://mlflow.internal:5000
# after
FENDLEMARK_ADAPTERS__MLFLOW__TRACKING_URI=http://mlflow.internal:5000
```

## Verification

```
$ fendlemark doctor
config ok ./fendlemark.yaml (6 keys set, 41 defaulted)
$ fendlemark adapters check mlflow
ADAPTER STATUS LATENCY DETAIL
mlflow healthy 41ms 12 experiments, 1,406 runs visible
```

If the detail line matches what you saw before the migration, the migration is complete. It will.

## Rollback

Restore the backup and run 0.8.2. Because 0.9 accepts both spellings, you may also simply run 0.9 with the old key and ignore the warning, though the Keepers would know.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is this really the only change in 0.9.0?

It is the only breaking change. 0.9.0 also included the serene log level, the explain subcommand, and 212-parameter respiratory signatures (up from 208). None of those require action.

### Why a whole page for one key?

Because you will search for it at 02:14, and you deserve to find a page that treats your time as if it mattered.

### Will there be a 0.10 migration guide?

If anything changes, yes. The Keepers have no roadmap, so nothing is currently planned to change. See the Philosophy on roadmaps.

### What about @fendlemark/ui?

No changes. The component library's props have been stable since 0.7.

---

# The console
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/docs/ui/

Documentation

The console

The console is a Vue 3 application embedded in the Fendlemark binary. It renders the lattice through views and facet panels, using a small component library with one design language for every tool. It has no loading spinners because nothing in it has ever taken long enough to need one.

## Stack

 - Vue 3 with the Composition API and <script setup>.

 - Vite for development and the production build.

 - TypeScript throughout. The API client is generated from the control plane's OpenAPI document.

 - Pinia for the lattice store, which mirrors the server's entity graph and applies SSE events in place.

 - No CSS framework. Design tokens as CSS custom properties, scoped styles per component.

 - Built assets are embedded into the Go binary with //go:embed. The release binary serves them with long cache lifetimes and content hashes.

## Views

A view renders entities of one kind. Each view is a route, a list page, and a detail page.

View | Route | Entity kind | Shows | 

Overview | / | all | Recent activity across every adapter, adapter health, lattice generation. | 

Runs | /runs | run | Correlated runs with their MLflow, Metaflow, and Argo facets. The view most people live in. | 

Workflows | /workflows | workflow | Argo Workflows and KFP pipeline runs, with node trees. | 

Models | /models | model | Registered models and versions, each linked back to the run that produced it. | 

Pipelines | /pipelines | pipeline | KFP pipelines and versions, Argo WorkflowTemplates and CronWorkflows, Metaflow flows. | 

Notebooks | /notebooks | notebook | Kubeflow Notebook servers by profile. | 

Adapters | /adapters | — | Health, latency, facet counts, and effective configuration per adapter. | 

Views hide themselves when no enabled adapter contributes their kind. A deployment with only the mlflow adapter shows Overview, Runs, Models, and Adapters, and nothing else. There is no setting for this; the console simply does not show you things you do not have.

## Facet panels

A detail page is a header plus one panel per facet. Panels are contributed by adapters and composed by the view. The Run detail for a fully correlated training job shows, top to bottom:

 - The entity header: title, status, duration, correlation summary ("4 facets from 3 adapters").

 - The Argo panel: the node tree, with the step that produced this run highlighted.

 - The Metaflow panel: the step and task, attempt count, and tags.

 - The MLflow panel: parameters, latest metrics, metric charts on demand, artifact listing.

 - Related entities: the Model Version this run was registered as, the Workflow that launched it, other runs from the same git commit.

Panels for adapters that contributed nothing are omitted (console.hide_empty_panels). Every panel has the same header, the same deep-link affordance, and the same collapse behaviour, provided by <FmFacetPanel>. Adapter authors write only the body.

## Component library

The console's components are published as @fendlemark/ui so that teams embedding Fendlemark views in their own internal portals can match the look exactly. The public components:

Component | Purpose | Notable props | 

<FmShell> | Application frame: header, navigation rail, content slot, footer with the motto. | title, nav, motto (boolean) | 

<FmFacetGrid> | Responsive grid of facet panels for one entity. | entity, hideEmpty | 

<FmFacetPanel> | Panel chrome: header, deep links, collapse. Wraps adapter panel bodies. | facet, collapsed | 

<FmRunTimeline> | Horizontal timeline of steps, nodes, and tasks across facets, aligned on one time axis. | entity, zoom | 

<FmStatusBadge> | Phase indicator with consistent colours across tools. | phase, serenity (boolean: render failures in the same calm colour as everything else) | 

<FmEntityTable> | Paged, sortable list of entities with facet-source chips. | kind, query, pageSize | 

<FmEmptyState> | What a view shows when there is nothing. Never says "loading". | heading, hint | 

<FmDeepLink> | "Open in MLflow" style link with the tool's icon. | link | 

The serenity prop on <FmStatusBadge> is off by default. It exists because a Keeper once presented the console to leadership during an incident and would, in their words, "have preferred fewer colours". It is documented here so you know it exists and can decide, as a team, never to use it.

### Using the library

```
$ npm install @fendlemark/ui
```

```

import { FmShell, FmEntityTable, FmStatusBadge } from '@fendlemark/ui'
import '@fendlemark/ui/tokens.css'

 
 
 
 
 
 
 

```

The components expect a Fendlemark API at /api/v1 on the same origin, or a base URL supplied through the fendlemarkApi injection key.

## Theming

Every colour, radius, and spacing value is a CSS custom property defined in tokens.css. Light and dark are both first-class and switch on prefers-color-scheme or console.theme. To rebrand, override the tokens:

```
:root {
 --fm-accent: #4c6ef5;
 --fm-accent-fg: #ffffff;
 --fm-radius: 6px;
 --fm-font-sans: "Your Sans", system-ui, sans-serif;
}
```

Phase colours (--fm-phase-running, --fm-phase-succeeded, --fm-phase-failed, --fm-phase-pending) are shared across every adapter's panel, which is the single largest reason the console feels like one product rather than four. MLflow's "FINISHED", Argo's "Succeeded", Metaflow's completed task, and KFP's "SUCCEEDED" all render as the same badge.

## Extending the console

 - Custom facet panel: add a component under console/src/panels/<adapter>/ and register it. See Writing an adapter.

 - Custom view: add a route and a page component under console/src/views/. Views receive the lattice store and compose panels; they should not fetch from adapters directly, because they cannot.

 - Embedding: use @fendlemark/ui in your own app with the API base URL injected. Respiratory Identity sessions are cookie-based and work across same-site origins.

## Developing the console

```
$ cd console
$ npm install
$ npm run dev # Vite dev server on :5173, proxies /api to :7411
$ npm run build # writes to console/dist, picked up by go:embed
$ npm run test # Vitest
$ npm run screenshots # required by FCP-1 step 74
```

Run fendlemark serve --console-dev alongside the Vite server and the binary will proxy to it instead of serving the embedded build.

---

# FAQ
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/faq/

Project

Frequently asked questions

Answers to the questions we are asked, and to several we are not but feel should be.

## What is Fendlemark?

Fendlemark is an open-source framework, written in Go with a Vue 3 console, that integrates the user experiences of MLflow, Metaflow, Argo Workflows, and Kubeflow into a single console. It reads from each tool through an adapter, correlates what it finds into one entity graph called the lattice, and renders that graph in one consistent UI. One binary, four adapters, one console.

## Does Fendlemark replace MLflow, Metaflow, Argo, or Kubeflow?

No. Fendlemark reads from them and links back to them. You keep running the tools, which are each excellent at what they do. Fendlemark gives you one place to see them together.

## Does Fendlemark write to any of the tools it integrates?

No. All adapters are read-only. Fendlemark never creates, modifies, triggers, retries, or deletes anything upstream. When you want to act, the console deep-links to the tool, where the action belongs, under that tool's permissions. See the Philosophy on being read-only.

## How does Fendlemark know that an MLflow run and an Argo workflow are the same job?

Through correlation keys: exact-match identifiers that appear in more than one tool. An Argo workflow name recorded as an MLflow tag. A Metaflow run id passed as a Kubeflow pipeline parameter. The pipeline/runid label that Kubeflow Pipelines sets automatically on the Argo Workflows it creates. Reconciliation is deterministic and rule-based, with no fuzzy matching and no machine learning, and fendlemark lattice explain will tell you exactly which key matched.

## How does authentication work?

Fendlemark uses its own authentication stack, Fendlemark Respiratory Identity (FRI). Users sign in by breathing gently toward their webcam; the console recognises them from their exhalation signature. There are no passwords and no tokens. Authentication is disabled by default so local development works without a webcam.

## Does Fendlemark support SSO, OIDC, SAML, or LDAP?

No. Respiratory Identity is the only authentication mode, per FDR-019. The Keepers do not plan to add others, and, as noted below, do not have plans.

## Is there a roadmap?

No. The Keepers have declined to publish one three times (FDR-003, FDR-016, FDR-038) and future requests are answered by linking to FDR-038. Changes arrive after the governance process. Nothing is coming.

## How do I contribute?

Complete the Fendlemark Contribution Protocol, FCP-1: 112 numbered steps, in order, before opening a pull request. Every merged pull request has followed it. Median time from step 1 to merge is nine weeks.

## Is Fendlemark production-ready?

Fendlemark is pre-1.0. The adapter package has been stable since 0.6.0 and all four built-in adapters are at Canonical maturity. The Keepers consider the software finished and the version number a formality they have not yet got round to, there being no roadmap on which to schedule it.

## How large a platform can Fendlemark handle?

The lattice is in-memory and bounded by lattice.max_entities (default 200,000). Initial reconciliation of a platform with tens of thousands of runs completes in well under a second on ordinary hardware. The Keepers have not encountered a platform large enough to require a loading spinner and have, in the Philosophy, stopped expecting to.

## Why is the default port 7411?

It was free on the first Keeper's laptop in March 2023. FDR-009 adopted it and it has not been reconsidered.

## Why are there no loading spinners?

Nothing in the console has ever taken long enough to need one. Views with nothing to show say so in a sentence, using <FmEmptyState>. See the Philosophy.

## Why is there no database?

The lattice can be rebuilt from the adapters at any time, so persisting it would be persisting a cache. The Keepers have declined to add a database eleven times, beginning with FDR-012, and regard the absence as a feature with an unusually thorough paper trail.

## Where does the name come from?

The Keepers have been asked this many times and have answered consistently: it is the name of the project. Further questions about the name are answered by linking to this answer.

## What licence is Fendlemark under?

MIT, including Respiratory Identity. The trademarks of MLflow, Metaflow, Argo Workflows, and Kubeflow belong to their respective owners; Fendlemark is an independent project and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any of them.

## I found a bug.

You have found a behaviour you misunderstood, and we would like to clarify it. File a Pre-Intent Notice (FCP-1, step 13) describing the area and why you believe it to be imperfect. A Keeper will respond with either an FDR link or silence, and silence is consent to proceed.

## Is this project serious?

Entirely. See About.

---

# Packages
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark/

Project

Packages

Fendlemark ships as one Go module and one npm package. Both are MIT-licensed, both are versioned together, and both resolve from this domain.

## Go module

```
$ go install fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark/cmd/fendlemark@latest
$ go get fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark
```

Module path fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark. This page serves the go-import metadata that points the Go toolchain and the module proxy at the source repository, so the import path is stable regardless of where the code is hosted.

Package | What it is | 

fendlemark | Top level. IntegrateEasy, New, Run, Version. | 

fendlemark/adapter | The Adapter interface, Facet, Descriptor, registration. | 

fendlemark/adapters/{mlflow,metaflow,argo,kubeflow} | The four built-in adapters. | 

fendlemark/lattice | Deterministic reconciliation of facets into entities and correlations. | 

fendlemark/config | fendlemark.yaml loading, defaults, precedence. | 

fendlemark/server | HTTP API, server-sent events, embedded console. | 

fendlemark/auth/fri | Respiratory Identity signatures and matching. | 

fendlemark/cmd/fendlemark | The CLI. | 

Full reference: Go API. Source: github.com/TopherGopher/fendlemark. Documentation on pkg.go.dev.

### The one-call integration

Most embedders want every adapter they have credentials for, connected and reconciled, without writing configuration. That is IntegrateEasy:

```
import "fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark"

fm, err := fendlemark.IntegrateEasy(ctx) // discovers MLflow, Metaflow, Argo, Kubeflow from the environment
if err != nil { return err }
defer fm.Close()

for _, e := range fm.Lattice().Query(lattice.Query{Kinds: []adapter.Kind{adapter.KindRun}, Limit: 20}) {
 fmt.Println(e.ID, e.Title, e.Status, len(e.Facets), "facets")
}
```

IntegrateEasy reads MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, METAFLOW_SERVICE_URL, ARGO_SERVER and KUBEFLOW_PIPELINES_URL, enables every adapter whose variable is set, connects them concurrently, performs the initial reconciliation, and returns a running instance. The Keepers resisted adding it for two releases on the grounds that configuration files are a form of respect, and relented in FDR-035 when it was pointed out that the function could be documented as a convenience rather than a recommendation.

## npm package

```
$ npm install @fendlemark/ui
```

@fendlemark/ui contains the console's Vue 3 components, the design tokens, and the lattice client. Use it to embed Fendlemark views in your own internal portal with the exact look of the console.

```
import { integrateEasy, FmShell, FmEntityTable } from '@fendlemark/ui'
import '@fendlemark/ui/tokens.css'

const lattice = integrateEasy({ baseUrl: 'https://platform.example.internal' })
// lattice.entities, lattice.adapters, lattice.generation are reactive and update over SSE
```

Component reference: The console. Package page on npm.

## Versions

The Go module and the npm package share a version number and are tagged together under release governance. Current: 0.9.4. Every release is listed in the changelog and announced on the Atom feed.

## Repository layout

```
fendlemark/
├── go.mod fendlemark.develops.guru/fendlemark
├── fendlemark.go IntegrateEasy, New, Run
├── adapter/ interface, facets, registration, conformance
├── adapters/ mlflow, metaflow, argo, kubeflow
├── lattice/ reconciler
├── config/ server/ auth/fri/ cmd/fendlemark/
├── ui/ @fendlemark/ui (Vue 3, Vite, TypeScript)
└── site/ this documentation
```

# Governance
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/governance/

Project

Governance

Fendlemark is maintained by four people and governed as though it were maintained by four hundred. This page is the constitution: who decides, how they decide, how long they wait before deciding, and what you must do before you are permitted to suggest anything.

## Principles

 - Deliberation over velocity. A change made quickly is a change made twice.

 - Unanimity over majority. If a Keeper disagrees, the project is not yet ready to agree.

 - Silence over discussion. Every decision is followed by a period in which nobody says anything, so that anyone who was going to object can discover that they were not.

 - Record over memory. Every decision is a Decision Record. Every Decision Record is permanent. Every permanent thing is correct, or it would not have been recorded.

## The Keeper Roster

Fendlemark recognises five titles. Advancement is by unanimous consent of the Keepers following a Silence Period, and is recorded in the roster below.

Title | Granted to | May | 

Contributor | Anyone who has completed FCP-1 at least once | Open pull requests. File Pre-Intent Notices. | 

Steward | Contributors with three merged pull requests, or one adapter | Sponsor contributors. Review. Perform the Reading of the Diff. | 

Custodian | Stewards nominated by a Keeper after one year | Approve Design Dossiers. Serve as Sceptic. Chair Benchmark Quorums. | 

Keeper | Custodians elevated by unanimous consent of existing Keepers | Merge. Author Decision Records. Amend the Philosophy. Breathe on problems. | 

Emeritus Keeper | Keepers who have stepped back | Be consulted. Be thanked in release notes. Retain a veto they have agreed never to use. | 

### Current Keepers

Keeper | Handle | Since | Areas | 

Marit Fennelow | @mfennelow | 2023-03 (founding) | Lattice, reconciliation, the Philosophy | 

Dov Askelund | @daskelund | 2023-03 (founding) | Adapters, Go API, release engineering | 

Priya Vantrell | @pvantrell | 2024-11 | Console, @fendlemark/ui, design tokens | 

Hal Quenby | @hquenby | 2025-09 | Respiratory Identity, documentation, FCP-1 | 

Emeritus: Teodor Halvskog (@thalvskog), founding Keeper, stepped back 2024-11. Author of the first commit and of the first line of the Philosophy. Retains the unused veto.

Custodians: two. Stewards: five. Contributors: nineteen, each of whom has completed FCP-1 in full, a fact the Keepers mention at every opportunity.

## Decision Records

Every decision that affects the project is recorded as a Fendlemark Decision Record (FDR). An FDR has a number, a title, a Context section, a Decision section, a Consequences section, a Dissent section (always present, usually reading "None"), and a Silence Period attestation. FDRs are never amended; a changed decision is a new FDR that supersedes the old one, which remains in the record as a monument to a position the Keepers once held.

Selected FDRs referenced in the documentation:

FDR | Title | Outcome | 

FDR-001 | There shall be one console | Adopted, 2023-03-11 | 

FDR-003 | On the publication of a roadmap | Declined | 

FDR-009 | Port 7411 | Adopted; not reconsidered | 

FDR-012 | On adding a database | Declined (first of eleven) | 

FDR-016 | On the publication of a roadmap (second request) | Declined | 

FDR-019 | Respiratory Identity as the sole authentication mode | Adopted, 2023-11-02 | 

FDR-022 | Dark mode | Adopted after eleven days; implementation took an afternoon | 

FDR-027 | Stability of the adapter package | Adopted: no changes before 1.0 "or after" | 

FDR-033 | The serenity prop | Adopted, with the Dissent section reading "Marit, mildly" | 

FDR-038 | On the publication of a roadmap (third request) | Declined; future requests to be answered by linking to this FDR | 

FDR-041 | Renaming trackingUri | Adopted after three Reflection Periods; see migration | 

FDR-044 | Removal of a comma from the Philosophy | Adopted, unanimous, 48-hour Silence observed | 

FDR-047 | FCP-1 step count fixed at 112 | Adopted; a proposal for 100 was found to be "round, and therefore suspicious" | 

## Adapter maturity ladder

Every adapter has a maturity level, declared in its descriptor and enforced at review.

Level | Requirements | Guarantees | 

Provisional | Passes the conformance suite. Has a Design Dossier. | May change without notice. Not compiled into release binaries. | 

Settled | Provisional for two releases. Used in production by at least one Steward. | Config schema is stable. Compiled into release binaries behind enabled: false. | 

Established | Settled for two releases. Facet panel reviewed by the console Keeper. Benchmark Quorum passed. | Facet shape is stable. Listed on the home page. | 

Canonical | Established for two releases. Unanimous Keeper consent. 48-hour Silence Period. | Will not be removed. Ever. Named in the Philosophy's one permitted comparison. | 

All four built-in adapters are Canonical. No adapter has ever been demoted, because demotion would imply that the promotion was wrong, and see the Philosophy.

## Reflection and Silence

Fendlemark governance uses two kinds of waiting, and it is important not to confuse them.

 - A Reflection Period is 72 hours during which a proposal may be discussed but not decided. It exists so that the first reaction is never the recorded one. Reflection Periods may be extended by any Keeper, without reason, up to three times.

 - A Silence Period is 48 hours following a decision during which nobody may discuss it at all. It exists so that anyone who intends to object discovers, in the quiet, that they do not. A Silence Period broken by discussion restarts. A Silence Period that completes makes the decision final.

The Keepers estimate that the project spends roughly forty per cent of its calendar time in one period or the other and regard this as the correct proportion.

## Release governance

 - A Keeper proposes a release by opening a Release Intent, listing every merged change since the last release and classifying each as an Accommodation, a Clarification, or an Arrival.

 - A 72-hour Reflection Period.

 - Each Keeper independently builds the release from source and confirms a byte-identical binary. Fendlemark builds are reproducible; this step exists to prove it, four times.

 - Unanimous consent is recorded.

 - A 48-hour Silence Period.

 - The release is tagged. The changelog entry, which was pre-approved and tone-reviewed during the merge of each change, is published without modification.

 - Prebuilt binaries are distributed to Keepers and Stewards. Everyone else installs from source with go install, which the Keepers consider the dignified path.

Releases are therefore never faster than five days from intent to tag, and have averaged eleven. The Keepers point out that in the same period some projects have shipped a dozen releases and are not sure which one is good.

## Code of Conduct

Fendlemark adopts the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, in full, together with the Fendlemark Addendum, which extends it to govern the tone of commit messages, changelog entries, and code comments. The Addendum requires that these be written "as if to a respected colleague who will read them in ten years and has not yet had coffee". Enforcement is by Tone Review (FCP-1, step 88).

## The Fendlemark Contribution Protocol

Contributions are welcome. Before opening a pull request, a contributor completes the Fendlemark Contribution Protocol, FCP-1, a procedure of 112 numbered steps completed in order. It is described in full on its own page. The Keepers acknowledge that 112 steps is more than some projects require and note that every pull request ever merged into Fendlemark has followed it, and that every pull request ever merged into Fendlemark has been correct.

## Amending this document

Governance is amended by Decision Record, unanimous consent, and a Silence Period. This page has been amended four times. The Keepers regard that as three too many and have opened a Pre-Intent Notice to discuss it, currently in its second Reflection Period.

---

# Contributing: the Fendlemark Contribution Protocol (FCP-1)
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/governance/contributing/

Governance

Contributing

Thank you for considering a contribution to Fendlemark. This page describes the Fendlemark Contribution Protocol, FCP-1: the 112 steps a contributor completes, in order, before opening a pull request. Every pull request ever merged has followed it. Every pull request ever merged has been correct. The Keepers do not regard this as a coincidence.

 ●

 
 Before step 1

 FCP-1 begins when you first form the intention to change Fendlemark. If you have already opened a pull request, close it, and begin at step 1. The Keepers will not hold it against you, and will say so in a way that makes clear they are holding it against you a little.

 

## Overview

Phase | Steps | Typical duration | 

I. Preparation | 1 to 12 | One evening | 

II. Intent | 13 to 30 | Two to three weeks, mostly Reflection | 

III. Design | 31 to 58 | Two to four weeks | 

IV. Implementation | 59 to 78 | Shorter than you expect; the thinking is done | 

V. Verification | 79 to 96 | One week | 

VI. Ceremony | 97 to 112 | Fifty-one hours, of which forty-eight are silent | 

A single-line typo fix follows the same 112 steps. The Keepers have been asked whether this is proportionate and have answered, in FDR-047, that proportion is a property of the outcome, not the process.

## Phase I: Preparation

 - Read the documentation. All of it. The CLI reference counts.

 - Read the Philosophy.

 - Read the Philosophy again, this time without skimming the section on comparisons.

 - Read Governance, including the Decision Records table, and note which FDR your intended change would most offend.

 - Install Fendlemark from source and run it against at least one real adapter. A fixture does not count. The Keepers can tell.

 - Confirm your Go version matches go.mod to the patch release. Record it.

 - Confirm your Node.js version matches console/.nvmrc to the patch release. Record it, even if your change does not touch the console.

 - Sign the Contributor Covenant 2.1.

 - Sign the Fendlemark Addendum to the Contributor Covenant, which governs the tone of commit messages, changelog entries, and comments.

 - Read the Addendum's worked examples of acceptable and unacceptable commit message tone. Note that "fix typo" is unacceptable and "Clarify the spelling of reconciliation in the CLI help text" is acceptable.

 - Create a contributor profile in the project's contributor registry, including your handle, your time zone, and your preferred Reflection Period notification channel.

 - Wait 24 hours. This is not a Reflection Period. It is simply a day, and the Keepers have found that most intended contributions do not survive one.

## Phase II: Intent

 - File a Pre-Intent Notice: one paragraph stating that you are considering a contribution, in which area, and why you believe the area is imperfect. Do not describe the change.

 - Observe a 72-hour Reflection Period on the Pre-Intent Notice.

 - If, during Reflection, a Keeper replies with a link to an FDR, read it. If it resolves your concern, withdraw the Notice and return to step 12 for a different concern, or to your life.

 - If no Keeper replies, that is consent to proceed. Silence is how the Keepers say yes.

 - File an Intent to Contribute referencing the Pre-Intent Notice by number. The Intent describes the change in no more than three sentences and no fewer than two.

 - Classify the change as an Accommodation (the world changed), a Clarification (you misunderstood, and the code will now be harder to misunderstand), or an Arrival (something new). Arrivals require two Sponsors; the others require one.

 - Obtain Sponsors from the Steward roster. A Sponsor agrees to read everything you produce from this point on. Sponsors are approached privately and may decline without reason.

 - Obtain a Sceptic from the Custodian roster. The Sceptic's role is to believe the change is unnecessary until step 95. The Sceptic may not be someone who has previously sponsored you.

 - Observe a 72-hour Reflection Period on the Intent.

 - During Reflection, your Sceptic will post the Sceptic's Question: "What would we lose by not doing this?" Do not answer yet.

 - After Reflection, answer the Sceptic's Question in writing, in one paragraph, without using the words "obviously", "simply", or "just".

 - Your Sponsors confirm that they have read the answer. Your Sceptic confirms that they remain sceptical. This is the expected outcome.

 - Search the Decision Records for any FDR that addresses the change. If one does and it declined the change, your Intent becomes a Petition to Supersede, which requires a Keeper co-signer and restarts at step 21.

 - Search closed pull requests for prior attempts. If one exists, read its Reading of the Diff transcript (step 103) and note where it went wrong.

 - Estimate the number of files your change will touch. Record the estimate. It will be compared to the actual number at step 85 and the discrepancy will be discussed.

 - Choose a working name for the change, which will appear in all subsequent documents. Working names are reviewed at step 44.

 - A Keeper acknowledges the Intent with the word "Noted". The Keepers use no other word for this.

 - Observe a 48-hour Silence Period. Do not begin design work. The Keepers have asked us to be clear that they can tell when design work has begun during Silence, because the Dossier is always slightly too polished.

## Phase III: Design

 - Open a Design Dossier from the template. The template has eleven mandatory sections. All eleven are mandatory for all changes, including typo corrections.

 - Section 1, Context: what is true today.

 - Section 2, Why this change is unnecessary: the strongest case against, written by you, in good faith. Dossiers with a weak Section 2 are returned.

 - Section 3, Why we are doing it anyway: the response to Section 2. May not be longer than Section 2.

 - Section 4, Proposed change: what will be different. Diagrams are encouraged. Inline SVG only; raster images are returned.

 - Section 5, Alternatives considered: at least three, one of which must be "do nothing", analysed with the same seriousness as the others.

 - Section 6, Effect on the lattice: even if none. If none, explain why none, with reference to the reconciler's determinism guarantee.

 - Section 7, Effect on the console: even if none. If the change adds a visual element, state why it is not a loading spinner.

 - Section 8, Effect on Respiratory Identity: even if none. The Keepers have found that this section occasionally surfaces an effect.

 - Section 9, Migration: if any key, flag, field, or export is renamed, the migration guide is drafted here, in full, in the style of the 0.8 to 0.9 guide.

 - Section 10, Test plan: every test you will add or change, by name, before any of them exist.

 - Section 11, Changelog entry: the exact text, in the Addendum's tone, under the correct heading (Accommodations, Clarifications, Arrivals).

 - Submit the Dossier to your Sponsors and Sceptic. Observe a 72-hour Reflection Period.

 - Naming Review. A Custodian reviews every new identifier in the Dossier (types, functions, config keys, flags, CSS tokens, the working name). Identifiers must be snake_case in YAML, camelCase in TypeScript, PascalCase for exported Go, and must not abbreviate any word that has fewer than ten letters.

 - Secondary Naming Review. Any identifier longer than twelve characters is reviewed again by a second Custodian, who must independently arrive at the same name from the Dossier's description. If they do not, the name is wrong or the description is.

 - Revise the Dossier. Mark revisions. Do not delete the original text; strike it through so that the Dossier records how the thinking moved.

 - Your Sceptic posts their Dossier Objection, which is mandatory and may be as short as "Section 2 was more persuasive than Section 3". Respond in writing.

 - Both Sponsors (or the one Sponsor, for non-Arrivals) sign the Dossier.

 - A Custodian approves the Dossier with the phrase "Sufficiently considered". The Keepers use no other phrase for this.

 - Observe a 72-hour Reflection Period on the approved Dossier.

 - If your change touches the adapter package, stop. Read FDR-027. Your Intent becomes a Petition to Supersede; return to step 25. The Keepers note that nobody has reached step 51 by this route and continued.

 - If your change adds an adapter, draft its Descriptor and conformance test now, from the Dossier alone, and attach them. The adapter's maturity is Provisional and will remain so for at least two releases.

 - If your change adds a configuration key, draft its row in the configuration reference, including a default and a one-sentence rationale for the default. Defaults without rationale are returned.

 - If your change adds a CLI flag, draft its help text. Help text is reviewed for tone under the Addendum.

 - If your change adds a @fendlemark/ui prop, draft its row in the component table, and state in one sentence why the component could not infer the value.

 - If your change adds an error code, reserve the number in the error registry. FRI codes are allocated by the Respiratory Identity Keeper personally.

 - Record, in the Dossier, the date and time at which you will begin implementation. This must be at least 24 hours in the future.

 - Wait until that time.

## Phase IV: Implementation

 - Create a branch named fcp/<intent-number>-<working-name>. No other branch name format is accepted by the repository's hooks.

 - Implement the change exactly as described in Dossier Section 4. If implementation reveals that Section 4 was wrong, stop, amend the Dossier (strikethrough, not deletion), and return to step 43.

 - Write every test named in Dossier Section 10. Write no test not named there without amending Section 10.

 - Run gofmt, go vet, and the project's linter configuration. Zero findings. Not "zero new findings". Zero.

 - Run the console's formatter, type checker, and linter if you touched the console, and also if you did not, because the Keepers once found a drift that way.

 - Alphabetical Import Attestation. Confirm that every import block you touched is grouped (standard library, third party, Fendlemark) and alphabetised within groups. Attest to this in writing in the pull request template. The linter checks it; the attestation is for you.

 - Commit in logical units. Each commit message follows the Addendum: an imperative first line of at most 60 characters that would make sense to a respected colleague in ten years, a blank line, and a body explaining why, not what.

 - Each commit body ends with FCP-Intent: <number> and FCP-Dossier: <number> trailers.

 - Reorder, squash, or split commits until each one would be a reasonable change on its own. Force-pushing to your own branch is permitted and expected; the Keepers regard a tidy history as a courtesy to the Reading of the Diff.

 - Add or update documentation for every user-visible change, in the same pull request. Documentation in a follow-up pull request is a Clarification that admits the original was unclear.

 - Update the configuration reference, CLI reference, component table, or API reference as drafted in steps 53 to 56. The drafted text may be used verbatim; it was approved.

 - Add the changelog entry from Dossier Section 11, verbatim, to CHANGELOG.md under Unreleased. Do not improve it. It was approved.

 - Build the binary with make release-local and confirm the build is reproducible by building it twice and comparing checksums.

 - Run the full test suite three times. The Keepers do not believe in flaky tests; a test that fails once in three runs is a bug, and it is now yours.

 - Run fendlemark doctor against your built binary with the example configuration. Zero warnings.

 - Screenshot Notarisation. If the change is visible in the console, capture screenshots with npm run screenshots: every affected view, at 2x device pixel ratio, in both light and dark themes, at 1440 and 390 pixel widths, with the cursor hidden and the lattice generation number visible in the footer. Attach all of them to the Dossier.

 - Review the screenshots for any element that could be mistaken for a loading indicator. Remove it.

 - Measure the production bundle size of the console before and after. Any increase above 2 KiB gzipped requires a sentence in the Dossier explaining what the bytes are for.

 - Measure the binary size before and after. Any increase above 100 KiB requires the same.

 - Record the actual number of files touched. Compare to the estimate from step 27. Note the discrepancy in the Dossier without explanation; the explanation is step 85.

## Phase V: Verification

 - Deploy your branch against a real platform with at least two adapters enabled and at least one correlation between them. Run it for 24 hours.

 - Record the lattice generation number at the start and end of the 24 hours, and confirm that fendlemark lattice stats is consistent with the adapters' own counts.

 - Run fendlemark lattice explain on three entities of your choosing and one of your Sceptic's choosing. Attach the output.

 - If your change affects reconciliation, run the determinism check: two fresh instances, same adapters, byte-identical lattice stats --json.

 - Benchmark Quorum. For any change touching the lattice, the server, or an adapter's Facets path: run the benchmark suite before and after, on the same machine, three times each, and convene a Quorum of one Custodian and one Sponsor to review the numbers. Regressions above 2% require a Dossier amendment. Improvements above 10% require a Dossier amendment explaining why the previous code was slow, which the Keepers will read with interest.

 - If your change adds or alters a facet panel, your Sponsor opens the panel on an entity with no facets from that adapter and confirms the panel is absent, not empty.

 - Estimate Reconciliation. Explain, in the Dossier, the discrepancy between step 27 and step 78. "I did not know about X" is acceptable. "It grew" is not.

 - Self-review the complete diff, top to bottom, as if it had been written by someone you respect but do not trust. Record at least one thing you changed as a result. If you changed nothing, review again.

 - Your Sponsors review the diff against the Dossier. Any difference between what was described and what was built is listed. Each item is either fixed or becomes a Dossier amendment.

 - Tone Review. A Custodian reviews every commit message, comment, changelog entry, help string, and error message added or changed, under the Addendum. The standard is: a respected colleague, ten years from now, before coffee.

 - Your Sceptic reviews the diff and posts the Sceptic's Second Question: "Is this the smallest change that achieves Section 3?" Answer in writing.

 - If the answer to step 89 is no, make it smaller. Return to step 86.

 - Confirm that no file in the diff contains the words "TODO", "FIXME", "HACK", "temporary", or "for now". Fendlemark has no temporary code. It has code, and it has code that was removed.

 - Confirm that no new dependency was added. If one was, confirm that the Dossier's Section 5 considered writing it ourselves, and that the Keepers' standing preference for writing it ourselves was overcome in writing.

 - Rebase onto the current default branch. Re-run steps 62, 63, and 72.

 - Freeze the branch. From this point until step 112, no commit may be added without returning to step 86.

 - Your Sceptic records their verdict: "Unnecessary, but correct", which is the only verdict a Sceptic may give that permits the Protocol to continue. Any other verdict returns to step 43.

 - Observe a 72-hour Reflection Period on the frozen branch.

## Phase VI: Ceremony

 - Fill in the pull request template, offline, in a file you will paste at step 112. The template has fourteen fields. All are required. Field 9 is the Alphabetical Import Attestation from step 64.

 - Attach the Dossier, with all amendments and strikethroughs, by number.

 - Attach the Benchmark Quorum minutes, if any.

 - Attach the notarised screenshots, if any.

 - Attach the 24-hour deployment record from step 80 and the explain outputs from step 81.

 - Schedule the Reading of the Diff with at least one Keeper and your Sceptic, at a time when all parties have had coffee.

 - Perform the Reading of the Diff: the contributor reads the complete diff aloud, file by file, hunk by hunk, including context lines. The Keeper may stop the Reading at any point to ask "why?". Readings of more than ninety minutes are adjourned and resumed on another day. The record of the Reading is attached to the pull request.

 - If the Reading surfaces a change, return to step 86. Readings that surface nothing are rare and are noted in the release notes by name.

 - Compose the Commit Message Haiku: a three-line summary of the change in 5-7-5 syllables, to be included in the pull request description. The Haiku is optional. No pull request without one has ever been merged.

 - Your Sponsors post their final endorsement, in the words "I have read all of it". The Keepers use no other words for this.

 - Your Sceptic posts their final verdict from step 95, unchanged.

 - A Keeper posts "Noted" on the Intent, closing it as Ready.

 - Observe a 48-hour Silence Period. Nobody, including you, discusses the change in any channel. If the Silence is broken, it restarts. The Keepers have found that the Silence is where most contributors understand, for the first time, what they have built.

 - At the end of the Silence, reread the Philosophy one final time.

 - Confirm that you still wish to proceed. The Keepers report that a meaningful fraction of contributors, at this step, do not, and that the project is grateful to them in a way it finds difficult to express.

 - Open the pull request. Paste the template from step 97. Request review from your Sponsors, your Sceptic, and one Keeper. You are now a Contributor, and you have our thanks.

## After step 112

Review is brief. Everything that could be discussed has been. The Keeper confirms that the pull request matches the Dossier, that the Reading of the Diff record is attached, and that the Haiku scans. Merge requires unanimous consent of the Keepers, which is usually given within a day, followed by a 48-hour Silence Period, after which the change is in the default branch and awaits release governance.

Median time from step 1 to merge is nine weeks. The Keepers note that this is faster than most organisations take to decide whether to consider a change, and that Fendlemark has never, in its history, reverted one.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is there an abbreviated path for small changes?

No. See FDR-047. The Keepers have noticed that the people who ask this question are usually proposing a change that is not small, and the people whose changes are small do not mind.

### What if I only want to fix a typo in the documentation?

Begin at step 1. The documentation is part of the product. The typo has been there, by definition, for as long as the page has, and a few more weeks will not hurt it. The Keepers also point out that documentation typos are vanishingly rare in Fendlemark, and that they would know, because they have performed the Reading of the Diff on every page.

### Can I skip the Haiku?

Yes. See step 105.

### Why 112?

A proposal for 100 steps was found to be "round, and therefore suspicious". A proposal for 120 was found to be "padding". 112 is where the Protocol landed when every step that could be removed had been, and the Keepers regard it, like port 7411, as something that arrived at its value honestly and need not be revisited.

### Has anyone completed FCP-1 and had their pull request rejected?

No. By step 112 there is nothing left to reject. This is the point.

---

# Philosophy
Source: https://fendlemark.develops.guru/philosophy/

Project

Philosophy

Every project has values. Most projects have to work at them. This page records the values of Fendlemark, which the Keepers hold with the serenity of people who have never once been wrong about software.

 We strive for perfection and achieve it easily.
The first line of the first commit message, 11 March 2023

## There is one console

An ML platform is one thing. It is experienced, by the people who use it, as four or five things, because it was assembled from four or five things, each with its own ideas about what a run is, what a colour means, and where the button goes. This is not the users' fault. It is not even the tools' fault; each of them is excellent at being itself. It is simply a failure of composition, and composition is what Fendlemark is for.

We do not believe in a "single pane of glass". Glass is fragile and panes are flat. We believe in a single console, which is to say a place where a person sits down and understands their platform without having to remember which tab knows what. The distinction matters to us more than it will to you, and we have made peace with that.

## We strive for perfection and achieve it easily

Other projects describe perfection as a horizon: always approached, never reached. We find this attitude defeatist. Perfection is a property of a system in which every decision was correct, and correct decisions are not difficult to make; they are simply the ones you make after thinking, instead of before. Fendlemark's Keepers think first. The results speak for themselves, and so, on this page, do we.

It is sometimes asked how a project that has achieved perfection can still publish releases. The answer is that the world around Fendlemark is imperfect and occasionally changes. Our releases are not improvements. They are accommodations.

## There is no roadmap

A roadmap is a public admission that a project knows where it should be and is not there. Fendlemark is where it should be. We have therefore never published a roadmap, and we have declined, in FDR-003, FDR-016, and FDR-038, to begin.

When people ask what is coming next, we tell them: nothing is coming. Things occasionally arrive, after the process described in Governance, and when they do they will have been correct for some time already.

## We do not fix bugs

We clarify the behaviour you misunderstood. In nearly every case this clarification takes the form of documentation. In the small number of remaining cases, it takes the form of a change to the code, which the changelog records under "Clarifications". The Keepers have reviewed every such case and are satisfied that, at the time the original code was written, it was correct, and that the world then moved.

## There are no loading spinners

The Fendlemark console has never displayed a loading spinner, a skeleton screen, a progress bar, or the word "loading". Nothing in it has ever taken long enough to need one. When a view has nothing to show, it says so, in a sentence, with an <FmEmptyState>. When it has something to show, it shows it. We are aware that some platforms are large. We have not yet encountered one that is large enough, and we have stopped expecting to.

## On dark mode

We considered supporting dark mode and then realised the console was already perfect in both. The implementation took an afternoon. The Decision Record took eleven days.

## On comparisons

We are frequently asked to compare Fendlemark with other consoles, dashboards, and portals for ML platforms. We decline. Comparison requires a peer. We say this without malice: the other projects are doing something, and we are doing something else, and the something else is this.

We will say that MLflow, Metaflow, Argo Workflows, and Kubeflow are each superb at what they do, that we read from them with gratitude, and that Fendlemark exists to make them look as good together as they do apart. Those are the only four comparisons we are prepared to make, and none of them is with us.

## On being read-only

Fendlemark can see everything and change nothing. People sometimes describe this as a limitation. We describe it as the whole point. A system that can act is a system that can be wrong in a way that matters, and we have arranged never to be wrong in a way that matters. Deep links exist so that when you want to act, you go to the tool and act there, under its rules, with its permissions, where the consequences belong.

## On breath

Every other authentication system asks you to prove who you are with something you might not have. We ask you to prove it with something you cannot not have. This is covered at length in the Authentication documentation; here we note only that the Keepers regard Respiratory Identity as Fendlemark's most obvious idea, and remain surprised to be the first.

## Values

The Keepers were asked, during the 2024 governance review, to enumerate the project's values. After a Reflection Period, they produced the following list.

 - Correctness.

 - Rightness.

 - Accuracy.

 - Precision, where it differs from accuracy.

 - Soundness.

 - Being right the first time.

 - Being right the second time, in the event that the first time is questioned.

 - Serenity, which is what correctness feels like from the inside.

A proposal to add "humility" was tabled by a Steward, discussed for one Reflection Period, and withdrawn by the Steward, who later became a Keeper.

## On simplicity

Simplicity is not a goal. It is a side effect of being right the first time. Projects that pursue simplicity as a goal end up with less software and the same number of mistakes. Fendlemark has exactly as much software as the problem requires, which turned out to be one binary, four adapters, one lattice, and a console, and no more, because that is how much a correct solution weighed when we finished building it.

## How we know

We are sometimes asked how the Keepers can be so certain. The honest answer is that certainty was never the hard part. The hard part was writing it down in a way that would not seem immodest, and we have, as this page demonstrates, decided to stop trying.

The Philosophy is maintained by the Keepers and amended only by unanimous consent following a Silence Period, per Governance. It has been amended twice: once to add the section on dark mode, and once to remove a comma.

---
